Models with reconciled forecasts

Source: R/hierarchy.R
reconciled.Rd

Wraps a model specification so that its forecasts are reconciled over a hierarchy every time it is forecast, also inside mt_backtest(). If the training data contain only the bottom strata, the aggregate strata are added with mt_aggregate_strata() before fitting, so that the base model forecasts every node; exposures for the forecast (exposure of mt_forecast()) can then be given for the bottom strata only, and those of the aggregates are their sums. Predictive draws (used by backtests) are coherent as well: given the reconciled rates, the Poisson variation of the deaths of the bottom strata is drawn independently per cell and draw (none for models of observed rates such as rwd(); for ensemble() and stratified() models as for the component or group each draw comes from; negative binomial for stanmomo(family = "nb")), and the aggregates are the sums of the bottom strata.

Usage

reconciled(
  spec,
  hierarchy,
  method = c("wls", "mint", "structural", "ols", "bottom_up", "proportional",
    "energy_score"),
  shrink = "auto",
  dependence = c("none", "ecc", "empirical", "auto"),
  fixed = NULL,
  years = 10,
  n_origins = 5,
  horizon = 5,
  control = list(),
  seed = 1,
  template = NULL
)

Arguments

spec

Base model specification (fitted to all strata).

hierarchy

An mt_hierarchy(). When the data hold the aggregate strata, their exposures are compared with those the hierarchy implies, with a warning (class mt_warning_hierarchy_exposure) when they differ, for example causes of death declared without additive = "rates".

method

A method of mt_reconcile(), or "energy_score" (score-optimal reconciliation, see Details).

shrink

See mt_reconcile().

dependence

"none" (default: the draws are reconciled as they are), "ecc", "empirical" or "auto" (the same as "none", kept for compatibility). With "ecc" the draws of the base model take the dependence of the draws of template before reconciliation (ensemble copula coupling, Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting 2013): the same as reconciled(coupled(spec, template), ...), see coupled(). With "empirical" the paths of separately fitted strata are reordered before reconciliation by a package-specific method (see mt_reconcile()). Draws of joint models such as li_lee() and tucker3(), which carry the dependence between strata, are never reordered by "empirical" (it then gives a warning and is ignored). The observation noise of predictive draws is independent across cells either way.

fixed

Strata whose forecasts are kept (see mt_reconcile()); not with "energy_score".

years, n_origins, horizon

Training of method = "energy_score": the length of the training window (the last years observed years), the number of inner origins in it (as in recalibrated()) and the number of years each inner forecast covers (horizons 1 to horizon, cut at the last training year).

control

Settings of the training for method = "energy_score": a list with any of n_draws (draws per inner forecast, default 100), draws_per_step (draws per training forecast in each step, 50), max_iter (number of steps, 500), eta (learning rate, 0.001), beta1 (0.9), beta2 (0.999), tol (1e-4) and epsilon (1e-8), as in ProbReco::scoreopt.control(). The optimisation stops early when no parameter moves by more than tol in a step, so tol must be below eta (0 runs all steps). max_iter = 0 gives OLS reconciliation.

seed

Random seed of the training for method = "energy_score" (inner forecasts, observation noise and the draws of each step), so that fits are reproducible.

template

With dependence = "ecc": the model specification whose draws give the dependence, usually a joint model such as cae() or li_lee().

Value

A model specification. With method = "energy_score" its fit holds $reconcile$scoreopt: d [bottom stratum, age], G [bottom stratum, stratum, age] on the scale of the reconciliation, the inner origins, the control settings and a table per age with the number of training forecasts, the scale of the bottom strata, the number of steps, and the mean in-sample energy score with OLS (energy_ols) and with the estimated \(d\) and \(G\) (energy_opt).

Details

Whether coherence costs accuracy, and which method and base model work best, depends on the data: compare them in a backtest at every level of the hierarchy (mt_score_table(..., hierarchy = )), as in the vignette "Coherent forecasts: totals and their parts".

Score-optimal reconciliation. method = "energy_score" follows Panagiotelis et al. (2023). The reconciled draws are \(\tilde y = S (d + G \hat y)\), where \(\hat y\) is a base draw of all nodes, \(S\) sums the bottom strata to the nodes, and \(d\) and \(G\) minimise the total energy score of past forecasts. Each time the model is fitted (also at every origin of an outer mt_backtest()), the base model is refitted at n_origins origins in the last years of the training data, as in recalibrated(), and forecasts the next horizon years. Every origin, horizon and age with observed values for all strata is one training forecast. \(d\) and \(G\) are estimated separately for each age, from the training forecasts of all origins and horizons, on the scale of the other methods (deaths, or rates when the levels share exposures). The estimation is stochastic gradient descent (Adam) started from OLS reconciliation, as in the package ProbReco. The score is that of the predictive distribution the forecast gives: reconciled draws plus the observation noise of the bottom strata. In the forecast, bottom values below zero are set to zero and the aggregates are their sums. The estimates and a table of the training are in the fit (see Value).

As in the paper (Section 6, Algorithm 1), \(d\) and \(G\) are free (no constraint such as \(G S = I\)), the objective is the total energy score with exponent 1 estimated from pairs of base draws (their Eq. 5), and Adam starts from OLS reconciliation with their settings (eta = 0.001, beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.999, epsilon = 1e-8, their Section 7). The gradient is written out analytically; ProbReco differentiates the same estimate automatically; with the same draws both follow the same optimisation path. The departures from the paper:

  • training forecasts: Algorithm 1 refits the base models on rolling windows of the length of the final fit at consecutive origins (250 one-step forecasts in their simulations), and the objective (their Eq. 4) is that of one horizon. Here the inner models use all training years up to each of n_origins origins (expanding windows, shorter than the final fit), and the forecasts of horizons 1 to horizon enter one objective, so that one \(d\) and \(G\) serve all horizons;

  • one \(d\) and \(G\) per age: every age is a hierarchy of its own;

  • the score includes the observation noise of the bottom strata, so it is the score of the predictive distribution of the deaths or rates;

  • draws_per_step is 50 by default (the paper uses 250 draws per score in its simulations), and the draws come from a fixed set of inner draws (see below);

  • stopping: the paper stops when the change in all gradients is less than 10% of eta; ProbReco and mortensor stop when no parameter moves by more than tol (1e-4, 10% of the default eta) in a step, or after max_iter steps (500, the default of ProbReco);

  • the rescaling before the optimisation and the bottom values set to zero in the forecast are package-specific (reference unknown). The paper does not treat negative values; the non-negative quadratic program of the projection methods (see mt_reconcile()) does not apply to the map \(S (d + G \hat y)\).

Two details differ from ProbReco. (1) Each step estimates the energy score from two samples of draws_per_step base draws of every training forecast, which ProbReco simulates independently. Here they are taken from the n_draws inner draws without replacement when there are at least 2 * draws_per_step of them, and otherwise from two disjoint random halves, so that a draw is never paired with itself (such pairs would contribute a distance of zero to the score). (2) Before the optimisation, the bottom values are divided by their mean observed value and every node, as an input, by its own mean observed value; the estimates are transformed back afterwards. This leaves the optimum unchanged, but Adam moves every parameter by steps of about eta, so the rescaling changes the path of the optimisation, and since it stops after max_iter steps or when the steps fall below tol, also the estimates, relative to ProbReco, which optimises on the original scale. The rescaling is package-specific; it makes the steps comparable across ages and between small and large nodes.

The method has many parameters and few training forecasts. \(G\) has one parameter per bottom stratum and node at each age (20 x 54 for 2 sexes x 2 regions x 5 quintiles with all aggregates); the defaults give about 20 training forecasts per age, which overlap. The only regularisation is the limited number of steps from the OLS start (control$max_iter, control$eta). \(d\) and \(G\) then fit the training forecasts much better than OLS, mostly through level corrections of single strata. These help in new years only if the errors of the training years recur: they do not after a change of trend, and the inner models are fitted to shorter series than the final model. In the package's backtests on simulated regional data and on the ONS data by sex and deprivation quintile, the method was less accurate than "wls" at every level of the hierarchy, also with fewer and smaller steps. The applications in the paper had longer training windows. Compare the method with "wls" or "mint" in a backtest before using it.

The training refits the base model at n_origins origins; the optimisation takes about 3 seconds per age for 54 strata with the defaults. control$max_iter = 0 gives OLS reconciliation at the cost of the inner forecasts.

References

Panagiotelis A, Gamakumara P, Athanasopoulos G, Hyndman RJ (2023). Probabilistic forecast reconciliation: properties, evaluation and score optimisation. European Journal of Operational Research 306(2): 693-706. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2022.07.040

Schefzik R, Thorarinsdottir TL, Gneiting T (2013). Uncertainty quantification in complex simulation models using ensemble copula coupling. Statistical Science 28(4): 616-640. doi:10.1214/13-STS443

Examples

x <- mt_example_regions(years = 2000:2019, regions = 3)
h <- mt_hierarchy(sex = "both", region = "all", quintile = "all")
fit <- mt_fit(reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "wls"), mt_aggregate_strata(x, h))
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
# \donttest{
# score-optimal reconciliation, trained on forecasts of 2012-2019 from 4 origins
es <- reconciled(lee_carter(), h, method = "energy_score", years = 8, n_origins = 4, horizon = 3,
                 control = list(max_iter = 200))
fit_es <- mt_fit(es, mt_aggregate_strata(x, h))
fit_es$reconcile$scoreopt$table
#>        age forecasts      scale iterations energy_ols energy_opt
